title: Alejandro Gómez Echavarría
section: A chirp in the fractional Fourier domain
text:
A chirp in the fractional Fourier domain
A linear chirp is a tilted streak in the time–frequency plane. The fractional Fourier transform rotates that plane by an angle α; when α lines up with the streak, the signal collapses into a narrow peak. That idea — optimal compactness — is the core of my research on frequency-modulated signals. Drag the sliders.

viewof c = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Chirp rate"})
viewof alphaDeg = Inputs.range([0, 180], {value: 30, step: 1, label: "Angle α (°)"})














s = 1.2
k = 4 * Math.PI ** 2 * s ** 2
M = [[1 / s ** 2 + k * c ** 2, -k * c], [-k * c, k]]
wigner = (t, f) => Math.exp(-(M[0][0] * t * t + 2 * M[0][1] * t * f + M[1][1] * f * f))
// Marginal on the rotated axis u = t·cosα + f·sinα is |X_α(u)|², a Gaussian with variance vᵀ(2M)⁻¹v.
varU = a => {
  const det = M[0][0] * M[1][1] - M[0][1] ** 2, ca = Math.cos(a), sa = Math.sin(a);
  return (M[1][1] * ca * ca - 2 * M[0][1] * ca * sa + M[0][0] * sa * sa) / (2 * det);
}
alpha = alphaDeg * Math.PI / 180
best = d3.range(0, 180.5, 0.5).reduce((b, d) => varU(d * Math.PI / 180) < varU(b * Math.PI / 180) ? d : b, 0)
spread = Math.sqrt(varU(alpha))


















































Plot.plot({
  width: 460, height: 460, marginBottom: 44, style: {fontSize: "13px"},
  x: {domain: [-3, 3], label: "time t", labelAnchor: "center", labelArrow: "none"},
  y: {domain: [-3, 3], label: "frequency f"},
  marks: [
    Plot.raster({x1: -3, x2: 3, y1: -3, y2: 3, pixelSize: 3, fill: "#3987e5", fillOpacity: wigner}),
    Plot.line([[-3.5 * Math.cos(alpha), -3.5 * Math.sin(alpha)], [3.5 * Math.cos(alpha), 3.5 * Math.sin(alpha)]],
      {stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "4 4", clip: true}),
    Plot.text([[2.6 * Math.cos(alpha), 2.6 * Math.sin(alpha)]], {text: ["u (α)"], dx: 14, fill: "currentColor"})
  ]
})






Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 240, marginBottom: 44, style: {fontSize: "13px"},
  x: {domain: [-3, 3], label: "fractional domain u", labelAnchor: "center", labelArrow: "none"},
  y: {domain: [0, 1.05], label: "|X_α(u)|² (normalized)", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(d3.range(-3, 3.001, 0.01), {x: d => d, y: u => Math.exp(-u * u / (2 * spread ** 2)), fill: "#3987e5", fillOpacity: 0.15, curve: "basis"}),
    Plot.lineY(d3.range(-3, 3.001, 0.01), {x: d => d, y: u => Math.exp(-u * u / (2 * spread ** 2)), stroke: "#3987e5", strokeWidth: 2, curve: "basis", tip: true}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.3})
  ]
})






md`Spread σ<sub>u</sub> = **${spread.toFixed(3)}** · most compact at α ≈ **${best}°**${Math.abs(alphaDeg - best) < 2 ? " — you found it." : ""}`

title: Framing the World
text:
When we try to make sense of the world — through science, education, or ideology — we inevitably use cognitive frameworks: ways of seeing and interpreting reality that shape what we consider true, important, or even real. Understanding these frameworks is essential not only in academia but in our everyday interpretations of politics, culture, and human behavior.
In this post I walk through some major cognitive frameworks and explore how a seemingly scientific theory — the theory of chaos — can challenge, complement, or even reshape how we think.

title: Framing the World
section: 1. The positivist framework: certainty through measurement
text:
1. The positivist framework: certainty through measurement
Positivism is one of the oldest and most influential worldviews in modern science. It assumes that:

Reality is objective and can be observed.
Knowledge comes from empirical evidence and the scientific method.
The world is predictable if we know its laws.

This framework works wonderfully in physics or engineering — but what happens when predictability breaks down?

title: Framing the World
section: 2. Enter chaos: a scientific challenge to predictability
text:
2. Enter chaos: a scientific challenge to predictability
The theory of chaos emerged from mathematics and physics to describe systems that are deterministic yet highly unpredictable due to extreme sensitivity to initial conditions.


Examples: the weather, brain activity, financial markets, ecosystems.
Chaos theory shows that small changes can lead to massive differences in outcomes, even if the system follows deterministic rules. In short: knowing the laws doesn’t always mean we can predict what will happen.
This poses a direct challenge to traditional positivism, undermining its assumption of predictability and control.

title: Framing the World
section: 3. Critical realism: a middle path between absolutism and relativism
text:
3. Critical realism: a middle path between absolutism and relativism
Critical realism, the philosophical framework developed by Roy Bhaskar, recognizes that:

There is a real world out there (it’s not just in our heads).
But our knowledge of it is always partial, socially conditioned, and open to revision.
Reality is stratified: not everything that exists is directly observable.

Chaos theory fits comfortably here. It supports the idea that reality is complex, layered, and sometimes beyond immediate empirical grasp, yet still real and knowable to a degree.






Unlike positivism, critical realism accepts uncertainty and complexity. Unlike extreme constructivism or relativism, it keeps a commitment to truth and objective reality.

title: Framing the World
text:
4. Constructivism and complexity thinking
In the constructivist framework, knowledge is built by individuals and communities — shaped by our experiences, cultures, and languages. Chaos theory is often used metaphorically here:

Learning is non-linear.
Small interventions can have big effects.
Systems (classrooms, societies, psyches) are dynamic and emergent.

This kind of thinking has influenced education, psychology, and organizational theory.

title: Framing the World
text:
5. Why this matters
Whether you’re studying education, building AI, or reflecting on politics, the frameworks you adopt shape your questions — and your answers. If we remain unaware of them, we risk:

Mistaking partial truths for total ones.
Silencing alternative perspectives.
Falling into ideological dogmatism — holding rigid views without room for critique or revision.

By learning from chaos theory and adopting frameworks like critical realism, we can embrace complexity without collapsing into relativism, and pursue truth without clinging to certainty.

title: Framing the World
text:
Final thought
The world is messy, unpredictable, and layered — but that doesn’t mean we can’t understand it. It just means we need better tools, deeper frameworks, and the humility to know that we’re always learning.
